title: A/B Testing & Statistical Power
interviewAnswer: A/B testing compares randomized groups to estimate causal treatment effects. Before running the test, define the primary metric, minimum detectable effect, significance level and required power to determine sample size.
why: A/B testing is one of the most common Data Scientist interview topics because it combines statistics, causal reasoning, product judgment and operational constraints.
intuition: Randomization makes treatment and control comparable on average, so a difference in outcomes can be attributed to the intervention rather than pre-existing group differences—assuming the experiment is executed correctly.
deepDive: Define the unit of randomization, primary metric, guardrails, minimum detectable effect, significance level, desired power and sample size before launch. Watch for interference between units, novelty effects, sample-ratio mismatch, repeated peeking and multiple metrics. Statistical significance is only one decision input; effect size, confidence interval, cost and risk matter too.
math:
Power = P(reject H₀ | a specified real effect exists)
Type I error = α
Type II error = β; power = 1-β
workedExample: For a checkout redesign, randomize users rather than page views if the same user can return repeatedly. Define conversion as the primary metric, latency/errors as guardrails, and decide the minimum lift worth shipping before estimating sample size.
commonMistakes: Stopping the test the first time p<0.05 without a sequential-testing plan.
Testing many metrics and reporting only the significant one.
Ignoring sample-ratio mismatch or users appearing in both groups.
followUps: How do you choose sample size?
How would you handle multiple testing?
What if randomization must happen by store or company rather than user?
production: Experimentation platforms need deterministic assignment, exposure logging, metric definitions, data-quality checks and safeguards against peeking. The statistical test is only one component of the system.

lab.goal: Estimate conversion uplift and a confidence interval before declaring an experiment winner.
lab.buildIt:
import math
n1,x1=5000,500; n2,x2=5000,575
p1,p2=x1/n1,x2/n2
d=p2-p1
se=math.sqrt(p1*(1-p1)/n1+p2*(1-p2)/n2)
lo,hi=d-1.96*se,d+1.96*se
print('uplift',d,'95% CI',lo,hi)
lab.useIt:
# scipy can provide a z-test or confidence-interval helpers; the key is
# to define the metric, unit of randomization and stopping rule before peeking.
relative=(x2/n2)/(x1/n1)-1
print('relative uplift',relative)
